questions.question: What is additive bilingualism?
options: Learning a second language while maintaining and developing the first
Replacing the first language with a second
Refusing to learn any new language
Speaking two dialects of one language
questions.explanation: Additive bilingualism means the second language is added to a maintained first language - associated with cognitive and social benefits.

questions.question: What is the opposite of additive bilingualism?
options: Subtractive bilingualism, where the second language gradually replaces the first
Multiplicative bilingualism
Passive bilingualism
Reflexive bilingualism
questions.explanation: In subtractive bilingualism, learning the new language comes at the cost of the first - often the result of assimilation pressure.

questions.question: What is language policy?
options: Decisions and rules about which languages are used in government, education, and public life
A list of forbidden words
A dictionary of official terms
A type of insurance
questions.explanation: Language policy covers explicit and implicit decisions about language use in public institutions, including which languages get official status.

questions.question: What is an example of official multilingualism?
options: A country granting legal status to several languages, such as Switzerland or South Africa
A country banning all foreign languages
A country with no laws at all
A school teaching only English
questions.explanation: Officially multilingual states give legal status to multiple languages; South Africa, for example, has eleven official languages.

questions.question: Is multilingualism unusual in the world today?
options: No - most of the world's population uses more than one language in daily life
Yes - almost everyone is monolingual
Yes - it exists only in Europe
No - because everyone speaks English natively
questions.explanation: Globally, multilingualism is the norm rather than the exception; monolingualism is largely a feature of some Western countries.
